stem: Why is calcitriol generally not recommended for treating simple vitamin D deficiency?

options.text: It is poorly absorbed by the intestine
It has a short half-life and cannot increase vitamin D stores
It is only effective when combined with high-dose vitamin D2
It requires activation by sunlight before it works
It is inactive until converted by the liver

explanation: Calcitriol has a short half-life and does not replenish body vitamin D stores, so it is not used for routine replacement in simple deficiency.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because calcitriol is absorbed adequately; the issue is that it is not suitable for building long-term vitamin D stores.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because calcitriol acts quickly but is cleared rapidly, so it does not increase the body's long-term vitamin D reserves.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because calcitriol does not need to be combined with vitamin D2, and this is not why it is avoided in simple deficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because calcitriol is already the active form of vitamin D and does not require sunlight activation.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because calcitriol is already active and does not need liver conversion before it can work.

source.hint: Think about the difference between providing a quick-acting hormone versus building up a storage reserve.
